header:
How Well Do You Really Know Carbon-Phosphorus Double Bonds?
In studying organic chemistry, we seem to restrict our understanding of the reactivity of carbon-phosphorus double bonds to their “metathesis” reactions with carbon-oxygen double bonds. With the assistance of transition metals, however, double bonds between carbon and trivalent phosphorus display distinctive modes of formation and reactivity. In this problem, whenever a subquestion asks for the SMILES of a complex, supplement it with a verbal description of the specific coordination mode.

header: Problem 6: Crystal Structures of Metal Superhydrides. On 2023-2-9, researchers from California State University published a study of metal superhydrides.

header_images.description: The image consists of three side-by-side crystal-structure diagrams labeled A, B, and C in black capital letters at their upper left. Each contains a unit-cell frame drawn with thin black lines, a pink ball-and-stick framework, and translucent colored polyhedra or spheres. In panel A, the black lines form an approximately cubic unit cell containing a large translucent blue cage-like polyhedron. Large dark-blue spheres occupy the cube center and all eight vertices. At the center is a polyhedral cage framework made of small pale-pink spheres and pink cylindrical bonds, defining the translucent blue polyhedron. On each face of the cube, pink spheres appear at positions near the middle left, middle right, upper middle, and lower middle. In panel B, thin black lines form an approximately cubic unit cell whose center contains a large translucent reddish-brown cage-like polyhedron. Large green spheres occupy the cube center and the midpoint of each edge. A polyhedral cage framework made of small pale-pink spheres and pink cylindrical bonds defines the translucent reddish-brown polyhedron. The framework contains two characteristic types of structural units. In-plane square units: near the inner side of every unit-cell face is a planar structure parallel to that face; 4 small pale-pink spheres at the upper-left, lower-left, upper-right, and lower-right positions on the side nearer the cell center form a small square. Vertex-directed tetrahedral units: viewed along a unit-cell vertex direction, the 3 pale-pink spheres nearest that vertex among the small squares on three adjacent faces form a triangular base. On the side of this triangle toward the unit-cell vertex is 1 pale-pink sphere outside the center of the triangle and not coplanar with it, with another 1 pale-pink sphere extending outward toward the vertex and bonded to it. These 5 spheres together form a tetrahedron-like unit containing a central atom. In panel C, thin black lines form an approximately hexagonal unit cell containing two overlapping translucent green cage-like polyhedra arranged diagonally from lower left to upper right, one in each of those regions. Each green polyhedron contains one large bright-green sphere near its center. The outer part of panel C is a continuous three-dimensional framework of pale-pink spheres and pink cylindrical bonds. Pink spheres lie around the edges and junction of the two green cages, and the pink bonds form multiple pentagonal, hexagonal, and oblique polygonal rings, resembling two connected or partially overlapping cages. The pink framework of the upper-right cage extends toward the upper-right and right edges of the cell, while that of the lower-left cage extends toward the lower-left and foreground regions. Overall, panel A is dominated by a blue cage polyhedron and blue spheres; panel B by a reddish-brown cage polyhedron and peripheral green spheres; and panel C by two translucent green cage polyhedra and two bright-green interior spheres. All three show the spatial relationship between the pink ball-and-stick framework and the unit-cell frame.

Kjeldahl Nitrogen Determination
Determination of nitrogen content has long been an important topic in analytical chemistry. In 1883, the Danish chemist Johan G.C.T. Kjeldahl invented the Kjeldahl method. The method mainly comprises digestion, alkalization, and titration: sulfuric-acid digestion converts the nitrogen in a sample into an ammonium salt; alkalization releases ammonia by distillation; and the absorbed ammonia is quantified indirectly by acid-base titration. header:
Semiconductors and Electrochemistry
Semiconductors are materials whose electrical conductivity at room temperature lies between that of conductors and insulators. Common semiconductor materials include silicon, germanium, and gallium arsenide. Based on band theory and Fermi statistics, doping with group V or group III elements, or with other materials that can donate electrons (donors) or accept electrons (acceptors), can regulate the Fermi level and carrier concentration of a semiconductor and thereby its various properties. Semiconductor carriers generally comprise electrons and holes. In this problem, involving an n-type semiconductor in which electrons are the majority carriers, only electrons need be considered. Nonuniform doping can create a carrier-concentration gradient in a semiconductor. The resulting diffusion causes charge separation and a built-in electric field; the built-in field opposes diffusion until equilibrium is reached. This is fundamentally similar to the electrochemical picture in which a chemical-potential difference drives charge transfer, which in turn produces a potential difference that opposes further charge transfer, ultimately establishing an electrode potential at equilibrium. By comparing a concentration-gradient-doped semiconductor with the electromotive force of an electrochemical concentration cell, this problem explores the universality of diffusion-electric-field equilibrium.
7.1 Built-in electric field and diffusion equilibrium in a semiconductor
Consider an n-type semiconductor at temperature T = 300 K with electron concentration varying with position x as $n(x)=N_{d0}\exp(-x/L)$. Here $N_{d0}=1\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, $L=0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, $D_n=225\ \mathrm{cm}^2\mathrm{/s}$, $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and $k=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$. These quantities are, respectively, the donor concentration at x = 0 (which, under the approximation used here, may be regarded as the electron concentration at x = 0), characteristic length, electron diffusion coefficient, elementary charge, and Boltzmann constant.

header:
Problem 3 Solid Electrolyte Interphase
The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) is an important research area in modern electrochemistry. During the first charging of a lithium-ion battery, the electrode potential lies below the reduction potential of the electrolyte, so additives and lithium salts in the electrolyte undergo electrochemical reductive decomposition at the solid-liquid interface. Insoluble solid products deposit on the electrode surface and form a passivation film that is electronically insulating but ionically conducting, thereby slowing electrode corrosion. Vinylene carbonate (VC), a classic film-forming additive, reacts preferentially and promotes formation of a high-quality SEI.

header:
Problem 6: Polysulfide Anions
A sodium-sulfur battery is a high-temperature molten secondary alkali-metal energy-storage battery that uses metallic sodium as the negative electrode, elemental sulfur as the positive electrode, and molten sodium beta-alumina as the solid electrolyte. It offers high energy density, inexpensive raw materials, and suitability for large-scale energy storage, and has become a research focus in electrochemical energy storage in recent years. Charging and discharging proceed through the formation of sodium polysulfides (Na_{2}S_{x}) with different chain lengths.

subquestions.text_open: 6.2 Sodium polysulfides (Na_{2}S_{x}) are key electroactive intermediates in sodium-sulfur batteries, and their anions can be synthesized and observed in the laboratory using common reagents. Under an N_{2} atmosphere, excess sodium tert-butoxide is added to a DMF solution of S_{8}, reducing S_{8} to polysulfide anion A. A disproportionates into another polysulfide anion B containing fewer atoms. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements show that some B anions undergo homolysis in solution to form bent anion C. C is trapped in zeolite cages in lazurite crystals, [(Na,Ca)_{4-8}(AlSiO_{4})_{6}(SO_{4},S,Cl)_{2}], and appears blue in solution. The sodium salt corresponding to polysulfide anion B is a common component of sodium-sulfur batteries. If it is heated to 300°C and melted, anion C dimerizes again to give isomer D of polysulfide anion B; the sulfur atoms in D occupy only two distinct chemical environments. 6.2.1 Give the chemical formulas of A and B.
6.2.2 Give the SMILES structures of C and D, showing the Lewis connectivity, and indicate the formal charge on every sulfur atom.
rubric: 1 point for the Lewis structure of C and 2 points for that of D; a reasonable resonance structure is also acceptable.

rubric_images.description: Lewis structures of C and D in the rubric. C is S_3^- with SMILES 'S=[S][S-]'; D is an S_6^{2-} isomer with SMILES '[S-]S(S([S-])=S)=S'.

subquestions.text_open: 6.3 Anion C can also be observed when S_{8} is dissolved in liquid ammonia, together with another hydrogen-free anion E. Early studies proposed the following mechanism: first, liquid ammonia undergoes autoionization to form NH_{2}^{-} and NH_{4}^{+}; second, NH_{2}^{-} attacks S_{8}, giving S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} by addition; third, S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} decomposes into cyclic anion F and a stable dibasic acid; fourth, F rearranges to form anion E and S_{8}, while the dibasic acid reacts with S_{8} and NH_{4}^{+} to form (NH_{4})_{2}S_{x}, which is subsequently converted into C. EPR measurements, however, show that anion F is not formed during the reaction. Moreover, the tendency of liquid ammonia to autoionize is extremely small and cannot explain the high solubility of S_{8} in liquid ammonia. Researchers therefore proposed a more plausible mechanism: first, S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} and NH_{3} participate in a proton-transfer equilibrium, forming S_{8}NH_{3} while generating NH_{2}^{-}, which promotes dissolution; second, NH_{3} can also react by nucleophilic substitution to form the small molecule S_{2}NH_{3}; third, S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} decomposes to anion B and intermediate G; fourth, G transfers all of its protons to NH_{3} to form anion H; fifth, H reacts with S_{2}NH_{3} to give anion E and NH_{3}, with all species in this reaction having a stoichiometric coefficient of 1. 6.3.1 Give the SMILES structures of E, F, G, and H, showing the Lewis connectivity. The Lewis structure of E is known to contain two S-S single bonds, and its sulfur atoms occupy two distinct chemical environments.
rubric: 1 point each for the Lewis structures of E, G, and H, and 2 points for that of F; a reasonable resonance structure is also acceptable.
